CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should signal willingness to engage in substantive negotiations while maintaining current retaliatory tariffs as leverage. We should not escalate further but should not concede either — the goal is to reach a face-saving deal that preserves our industrial policy space and tech development trajectory. We should offer concrete purchase commitments (agricultural goods, energy) as a gesture while holding firm on structural issues like Made in China 2025 and state subsidies.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is real but not yet existential. The US has imposed tariffs on $250 billion of Chinese goods (roughly half of bilateral trade), and Trump has threatened to tariff the remaining $267 billion, which would cover virtually all US-China trade (Fox Business, Sept 2018). China has retaliated on $110 billion of the $130 billion in US imports, leaving almost no further retaliatory room. The 10% tariffs were set to rise to 25% at end of 2018, creating near-term economic pressure. However, as Brookings notes, China's exports are largely assembled goods in global value chains where more than half the value comes from other countries (South Korea, Japan), meaning the direct hit to China's GDP is moderated. China's retaliatory tariffs on US agricultural products (soybeans down 20%) and automobiles are already causing political pain in US swing states, giving us leverage. The Washington Post reports that Chinese leaders feel betrayed after multiple failed deals (with Ross, then Mnuchin), suggesting the US negotiating posture is unreliable — this counsels caution about concessions but also signals that a deal is possible if we can find a trustworthy channel. The Xi-Trump dinner at G20 (Dec 1, 2018) produced a 90-day truce, and as of Dec 20, we are within that window. This is the moment to negotiate seriously, not to escalate or to fold. Escalation risks triggering the full $267 billion tariff threat; concession risks undermining our long-term tech ambitions. The optimal path is to offer near-term purchase commitments (which cost little structurally) while protecting our core industrial policy space.
key_factors: US tariffs cover $250B of Chinese goods, with threat to tariff remaining $267B
China has retaliated on $110B of $130B in US imports — limited further retaliatory capacity
10% tariffs scheduled to rise to 25% at end of 2018, creating near-term pressure
China's role in global value chains means direct GDP impact is moderated (Brookings analysis)
US agricultural sector (soybeans, autos) already suffering, creating political leverage for China
G20 dinner (Dec 1, 2018) produced 90-day truce — negotiations window is open
Chinese leaders feel betrayed after failed deals with Ross and Mnuchin (Washington Post)
China lowered tariffs on non-US goods to redirect trade away from US suppliers

sources_cited.excerpt: Effective Sept. 24, President Trump announced a 10% tariff on $200 billion in Chinese imports. That tariff is currently 10%, but at the end of 2018, that's expected to rise to 25%... President Trump has also indicated that if things don't go as to what he wants to happen, he's going to do it on the rest of it... $267 billion worth of imports. For all intents and purposes, that would put a tariff in place on 100% of U.S.-China trade

Smartphones come to the U.S. as exports from China even though there are thousands of parts produced and assembled in many countries... more than half of the value of those products are in parts and components from other countries like South Korea and Japan

Chinese leaders believed they had a trade agreement last year with Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross, only to see President Trump veto it. In May, they reached a second deal with Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, but Trump again turned thumbs down — this time via Twitter

China also announced some tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods... This second round of Chinese tariffs is going to now cover $110 billion of the $130 billion of U.S.-China trade -- again, almost 100% of the entire trading relationship
